nodes.title: What's the best way to keep a business knowledge base up to date in Flowise?
nodes.body:
Hi everyone,

I'm building a Flowise assistant for a real service-based business and one challenge I'm running into is keeping the knowledge base synchronized as content changes.

The business website includes:

Service pages
FAQs
Pricing information
Blog articles
Location-specific content

I'm trying to decide between a few approaches:

Re-index the entire knowledge base on a schedule.
Update only pages that have changed.
Separate FAQs from long-form articles.
Keep structured business data outside the vector store and retrieve it differently.

For those running Flowise in production:

How do you keep business content updated?
Do you separate static and frequently changing content?
Have you found a workflow that scales well as the website grows?

I'd appreciate hearing about real-world implementations.

Small update after a few more days of testing.

I've moved away from treating the entire website as one collection and started separating service pages, FAQs, blog articles, and location pages into different document groups. Retrieval quality has been much more consistent for customer support questions, especially when the assistant needs to distinguish between evergreen information and content that changes more frequently.

For anyone interested, [the website I'm testing](https://junkremovalbeavertonor.com/) with is a real local service business rather than a synthetic dataset, so it includes service pages, FAQs, pricing information, location-specific content, and long-form guides. Using real business content has exposed edge cases that never appeared when I was testing with sample documents.

My next step is comparing incremental updates against scheduled full re-indexing to see which approach scales better as the site grows.

If anyone has implemented automatic change detection or selective re-indexing in Flowise, I'd still love to hear how you approached it in production.

nodes.title: Eden AI Gmail Assistant – Email Summary + Draft + Reply
nodes.body: Hi everyone, I built this chatflow that retrieves the latest unread Gmail emails, summarizes and analyzes their content with Eden AI, then creates a Gmail draft reply for the user to review before sending. Features: - Reads unread Gmail messages - Summarizes / analyzes content via Eden AI (OpenAI-compatible EU endpoint) - Generates a draft reply (never sends automatically — human reviews first) Setup: you just need a Gmail OAuth credential and an Eden AI API key, set as a Flowise variable. I've also opened a PR to add it to the marketplace: [LinkChart](https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/pull/6555) Screenshot and JSON attached below :

This is a practical Flowise use case.

I especially like that the workflow only creates a Gmail draft and keeps the final send action under human review. For email automation, that safety boundary matters a lot.

A few metrics I would probably track if this runs regularly:

* cost per processed email
* cost per useful draft
* latency from unread email to draft
* retry rate when Gmail or the model call fails
* token usage for long email threads
* whether attachments are excluded or summarized separately
* draft quality / edit distance before sending
* provider timeout or rate-limit frequency
* whether sensitive email content is routed only through approved endpoints

Since this uses an OpenAI-compatible EU endpoint, the provider boundary is also important. Email workflows are more sensitive than normal chatbot prompts, so it helps to make the data path very explicit: what content is sent to the model, what is stored, and what remains only in Gmail.

For production use, I think the key question is not only whether the assistant can summarize one email, but whether it can process many emails reliably with predictable cost, latency, and human review control.

nodes.title: Survey: Does your AI agent have an identity problem?
nodes.body:
Hi everyone 👋

I'm reaching out to the AI agent community because I think we're all heading toward the same problem, and I'd love your input.

**The question we're exploring:**

> Every SaaS platform has user accounts — for humans. But when your AI agent calls an API, it borrows a human's credentials. The AI itself has no identity.

If you're building AI agents that call external services (Shopify, Slack, Notion, GitHub, etc.) — how are you handling authentication across multiple platforms right now?

We've put together a **short 3-minute survey** to collect experiences from people who've hit this wall (or think they will). No sign-up, no product pitch — just honest questions to understand how the community is handling this:

🔗 **[Take the survey →](https://nexus-7xp6n.ondigitalocean.app/static/survey.html)**

I'd really appreciate if you could spare a few minutes to share your thoughts. I'll share the results openly once we have enough data.

Thank you! 🙏

This is a really interesting discussion. I think identity and authentication are definitely important, but once an AI agent gets access to an account, the next challenge is making sure it doesn't make costly mistakes.

I've been exploring an open-source project called FailproofAI, and one thing I like is that it focuses on catching common agent failures at runtime. Things like getting stuck in loops, repeatedly making the same failing call, exposing sensitive information, or attempting risky actions can be detected and handled before they become bigger problems.

If anyone's curious, the docs explain the idea pretty well: "docs.befailproof.ai" (https://reference-url-citation.invalid/0).

I feel like combining solid authentication with safeguards like these is probably the direction many production AI systems will end up taking.

nodes.title: Feature: Memory Poisoning (ASI06) Protection for AI Agent Nodes — OWASP Reference
nodes.body:
## Memory Poisoning (ASI06) in Flowise AI Agent Flows

Flowise is increasingly used to build production AI agent workflows where agents read from external sources (web scraping, email parsing, document ingestion) and write results into memory or pass them to downstream nodes.

This creates a critical attack surface known as **ASI06 — Memory Poisoning**, defined in the [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2025](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/).

**The attack:** A malicious payload embedded in an external source (e.g., a webpage, email, or document) is processed by a Flowise agent and written into the flow's memory. Downstream nodes then execute based on the poisoned memory, leading to data exfiltration or full workflow compromise.

## OWASP Agent Memory Guard

The [OWASP Agent Memory Guard](https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agent-memory-guard) project provides a lightweight Python reference implementation of a scan-before-write pattern that addresses this exact threat:

```python
from agent_memory_guard import MemoryGuard, GuardPolicy

guard = MemoryGuard(policy=GuardPolicy.BLOCK)
result = guard.scan(external_content)
if result.is_safe:
    agent_memory.write(result.sanitized_content)
```

It is already being discussed and adopted by maintainers of LangGraph, LiteLLM, AutoGen, and other major frameworks.

Would the Flowise team be open to:
1. Adding a reference to this pattern in the Flowise security docs
2. Optionally integrating a memory validation step in the AI Agent node pipeline

Happy to provide more technical detail or a prototype integration.

nodes.title: Add GoodMem as a Memory / Knowledge-base Node
nodes.body:
[GoodMem](https://goodmem.ai/) is a memory layer for AI agents with support for semantic storage, retrieval, and summarization. GoodMem supports built-in OCR for PDF and DOCX files, so documents can be uploaded directly and turned into searchable memories without a separate ingestion pipeline. It is self-hostable, so your data stays on your own infrastructure, and it is model-agnostic — you bring your own embedder, reranker, and LLM (OpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, local models, …) and swap them per space without re-architecting. On top of that it offers multi-space semantic search (one retrieval call across many knowledge bases), full CRUD over spaces and memories with metadata, and a single API that ties embeddings, chunking, retrieval, and reranking together.


Why add it to Flowise?
Flowise already has great building blocks for chatflows and agents, but persistent, queryable memory across files/emails/web content usually means stitching together a vector DB + embedder + reranker + ingestion pipeline yourself. A GoodMem node would give Flowise users that whole stack as one node they can drop into any flow.

Key perks:

 - Self-hostable — run GoodMem on your own infra, keep your data in your network.
 - Bring-your-own models — choose the embedder, reranker, and LLM per space; swap them later without re-architecting.
 - Built-in OCR for PDF & DOCX — upload files directly as memories, no extra ingestion node needed.
 - Multi-space semantic search — one retrieval call can span many knowledge bases at once.
 - Full CRUD — spaces and memories are first-class, with metadata, filters, and lifecycle management.
Proposed Node


A single GoodMem node in the Tools category, backed by a GoodMem API credential (Base URL + API Key + Verify SSL). The node exposes 11 actions and the Default Embedder and Default Space selectors are pulled live from the connected GoodMem server, so users pick from real options instead of typing IDs. Agents can search across one or multiple spaces in a single call and manage the full lifecycle of spaces and memories from inside a Chatflow or Agentflow.

Actions: List Embedders, List Spaces, Get Space, Create Space, Update Space, Delete Space, Create Memory, List Memories, Get Memory, Retrieve Memories, Delete Memory.

Example Scenario
Build a self-hosted "ask my stuff" agent in Flowise:

Spin up GoodMem on your own server and create a space using your preferred embedder and reranker.
Ingest your emails, Google Drive files, and PDFs as memories (GoodMem OCRs PDF/DOCX on the way in).
In a Flowise Agentflow, wire the GoodMem node alongside your chosen LLM node.
The agent calls Retrieve Memories to semantically search across the relevant spaces, then the LLM summarizes the results — all running on infrastructure you control.

nodes.title: Asking for Guidance
nodes.body:
Hey everyone! 👋
I'm Umesh, a full-stack developer from India. I work with MERN stack and Java backend. I've previously contributed to OWASP Dependency Check and have 2 merged PRs there.
I'm really excited about Flowise and want to start contributing here. I went through some issues but wanted to connect with the community first before jumping in.
A few questions:

Which areas need the most help right now?
Any good first issues you'd recommend for someone new to the codebase?
Any tips for setting up the dev environment quickly?

Looking forward to contributing and learning from this community!

For a MERN/Java background, I would start with areas where you can contribute without needing to understand the entire Flowise internals on day one:

1. documentation gaps from real setup/use
2. small UI fixes in the node configuration forms
3. new examples/templates for common RAG or agent flows
4. tests or bug fixes around existing nodes/connectors
5. validation/error-message improvements for credentials and node inputs

For first issues, I would look for problems where the expected behavior is already clear. Good examples are:

- a node accepts invalid config and fails later
- the UI error message does not explain which credential/input is missing
- docs are missing one required env var or setup step
- an integration works but lacks a minimal example

Those are usually better first contributions than adding a brand-new integration, because a new node often touches UI schema, credentials, runtime execution, docs, and tests at the same time.

For setup, I would do this first:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise.git
cd Flowise
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm start
```

Then pick one existing node close to what you want to work on and trace it end-to-end:

```text
credential definition
node UI inputs
runtime execution
docs/example
tests if present
```

Given your OWASP Dependency Check background, security-adjacent contributions could be especially useful: safer credential validation, clearer handling of missing secrets, dependency/update notes, or examples that avoid leaking keys in logs.

The best first PR is usually small and boring: one reproducible problem, one focused fix, and a short before/after explanation.

nodes.title: AI-Powered Organizational Policy Assistant using Flowise RAG
nodes.body: # AI-Powered Organizational Policy Assistant using Flowise I developed a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) based organizational policy assistant using Flowise, LangChain, and OpenAI. The system enables users to upload organizational policy documents and interact with them using natural language queries. Instead of relying on general model knowledge, the assistant retrieves relevant policy sections through semantic vector search and generates grounded responses based strictly on the uploaded documents. ## Key Features * PDF policy document ingestion * Recursive text chunking for document processing * OpenAI embeddings for semantic similarity search * Vector-based retrieval using an in-memory vector store * Grounded response generation with hallucination control * Conversational querying of organizational policies * Prompt engineering rules to reduce unsupported assumptions ## Potential Organisational Use Cases This type of assistant can be adapted for several real-world organisational scenarios, including: * HR policy and employee handbook assistants * Internal IT support knowledge assistants * Compliance and governance document retrieval * Health and safety policy guidance * Employee onboarding support systems * Internal knowledge base assistants * Standard operating procedure (SOP) querying systems ## Technology Stack * Flowise * LangChain * OpenAI GPT-4.1-mini * OpenAI Embeddings (`text-embedding-3-small`) * In-Memory Vector Store ## RAG Workflow 1. Policy documents are uploaded into the system 2. Documents are split into smaller chunks 3. Chunks are converted into embeddings 4. Embeddings are stored in a vector database 5. Relevant document sections are retrieved based on user queries 6. GPT generates grounded responses using only the retrieved context To improve reliability, I implemented prompt rules to: * restrict the model to the * prevent hallucinations * avoid unsupported assumptions * ensure responses remain policy-grounded Screenshots and exported chatflow JSON are attached below. [AI-Powered Organizational Policy Assistant Chatflow.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27731385/AI-Powered.Organizational.Policy.Assistant.Chatflow.json)

Nice use case. For a policy assistant, I would add evaluation around retrieval, not only prompt rules around generation.

The failure mode I would test first is: “the answer sounds grounded, but the retrieved section was the wrong policy section.” Prompt instructions can reduce hallucination, but they cannot fix weak retrieval.

A useful eval set for this kind of assistant usually has rows like:

```text
question
expected_policy_document
expected_section_or_clause
acceptable_answer
should_abstain
```

Then score separately:

- retrieval hit: did the right policy section appear in top-k?
- citation correctness: did the answer cite the section it actually used?
- abstention: did it say “not found in policy” when the answer is absent?
- conflict handling: what happens when two policy versions disagree?

For production I would also avoid an in-memory vector store unless this is only a demo. Policy documents are versioned artifacts, so storing `document_id`, `policy_version`, `effective_date`, and `department` as metadata will make the assistant much safer when policies change.

nodes.title: Idea: Add Xquik public X/Twitter data nodes
nodes.body:
Flowise already supports custom tools and third-party components. A native Xquik integration would give builders reusable read-only public X/Twitter data nodes without pasting REST calls into custom function nodes.

Suggested first version:

- Credential: Xquik API key, stored as a password field.
- Search Tweets: `GET /x/tweets/search`
- Get Tweet: `GET /x/tweets/{id}`
- Get User: `GET /x/users/{id}`
- Search Users: `GET /x/users/search`
- List User Tweets: `GET /x/users/{id}/tweets`
- Get Trends: `GET /x/trends`

Useful flows:

- Query or trend -> summarizer -> Slack, Sheets, or webhook
- Profile lookup -> lead or account enrichment
- Recurring public research reports

Docs:

- https://docs.xquik.com/api-reference/overview
- https://github.com/Xquik-dev/x-twitter-scraper

Suggested scope: read-only public data first. I would avoid posting, likes, follows, DMs, and profile updates in the initial node set.

If this fits the Flowise component model, I can help with a PR that includes a credential definition, co-located tests, and docs following the contribution guide.

Read-only first is the right scope.

For a Flowise node like this, I would make provenance part of the output contract from day one. Downstream RAG/agent flows need to know where a tweet/user/trend came from, not just the text.

For example, every output item should probably include:

```json
{
  "source": "xquik",
  "resource_type": "tweet",
  "id": "...",
  "url": "...",
  "author_id": "...",
  "created_at": "...",
  "retrieved_at": "...",
  "query": "...",
  "rate_limit": {
    "remaining": 123,
    "reset_at": "..."
  }
}
```

That makes the node much easier to use in research/reporting flows because the final answer can cite the original public URL and the workflow can debug stale data.

I would also keep posting/likes/follows/DMs out of the initial version. Search/read nodes plus credentials, pagination, rate-limit metadata, and docs examples would already be useful and much lower risk.

Thanks, this is useful guidance. I agree the first version should stay read-only and make provenance explicit instead of returning opaque text.

I will scope any implementation around search/read nodes, credentials, pagination, docs examples, and normalized output items with source, resource_type, public URL, IDs, created/retrieved timestamps, query context, and rate-limit metadata only where the API response or headers expose it. I will also leave posting, likes, follows, and DMs out of the first pass.

nodes.title: File Uploads passing all the data to LLM Node
nodes.body:
My use case is, user uploads one image and one document file in the initial chat. I have 2 MCP tool nodes, one handles image and other handles document. After that I pass the small output received from these 2 MCP tool nodes to LLM node. 

The issue is Flowise is sending all the uploaded image and document data as base64 string to LLM node and its erroring out. Because the context of model in LLM node is 32k. I am using Llama 3.1 8B Instruct model. 

How to stop this from happening. Already MCPs have consumed the image and document extracted the required info. Don't want file upload data to get passed into the LLM node.

I want user to upload these 2 files (they can upload any image or document) so I can't use RAG as well.

This is a real issue because once file contents and MCP tool outputs both keep flowing forward, the LLM node ends up paying for context it does not actually need. If the useful result is already extracted upstream, the raw file payload should ideally stop there.

A practical fix might be an explicit transformation step between the MCP stage and the LLM node that keeps only the structured result fields. That would give you more predictable context size and make the graph easier to reason about when multiple files are involved.

This sounds like the file is being passed into the LLM path too directly.

For RAG you generally want two separate stages:

1. ingestion: upload -> parse -> chunk -> embed -> store in vector store
2. QA: user question -> retrieve top-k chunks -> send only those chunks to the LLM

If the whole uploaded file is attached to the LLM node, the model can see far more context than intended, and you also lose control over token cost and data exposure.

I would check the generated prompt or tracing output for the LLM call. If you see the entire file contents there, move the file handling before the LLM node and route it through a document loader/vector store first.

A safer production shape is:

```text
File Upload
  -> Document Loader
  -> Text Splitter
  -> Embeddings
  -> Vector Store

Chat Input
  -> Retriever(topK, metadata filters)
  -> Prompt Template
  -> LLM
```

Also add metadata filters if files belong to different users/sessions. Retrieval should be scoped by `user_id`, `session_id`, or `document_id`, otherwise one flow can accidentally retrieve another flow's chunks.

This is a common pain point! At RevolutionAI (https://revolutionai.io), we have solved the formatting vs logging dilemma a few ways:

**Option 1: Separate post-processing chains**
Run formatting and logging as parallel branches after the main response, not sequential.

**Option 2: Middleware approach**
Intercept the raw response, clone it — one copy goes to formatting, one to logging. Both complete independently.

**Option 3: Async logging**
Log asynchronously so it does not block the formatted response. Fire-and-forget pattern.

```python
# Pseudo-pattern
raw_response = get_llm_response()

# Fire logging async (non-blocking)
asyncio.create_task(log_response(raw_response))

# Return formatted immediately
return format_response(raw_response)
```

The key insight: logging should never be in the critical path of user response.

nodes.title: Feature Request: Ability to Disable Nodes (Comment-Out / Toggle Execution)
nodes.body:
## Problem
When building complex flows, there is currently no way to temporarily disable a node without deleting it or rewiring the graph. This makes iterative development, debugging, and experimentation unnecessarily destructive.

As developers, we often want to:
- Test alternate logic paths
- Temporarily bypass expensive or unstable nodes (LLMs, tools, APIs)
- Debug upstream behavior without losing downstream structure
- Keep experimental or reference nodes in the canvas without execution

Right now, deleting or disconnecting nodes breaks flow continuity and configuration history.

## Proposed Solution
**Introduce a “Disable Node” capability, similar to commenting out code.**

## Critical Execution Semantics (Must Be Explicit)
A disabled node should clearly affect downstream execution in one of the following deterministic ways:

## 1: Hard Stop / Branch Termination (Preferred)
- A disabled node cannot produce outputs
- Any edges leaving the node are considered inactive
- All downstream nodes depending on that node are implicitly disabled or skipped
- Execution logs clearly indicate where the flow was halted

## 2: Explicit Disallow of Connections
- A disabled node cannot have outgoing connections
- Existing outgoing connections are visually disabled and ignored at runtime
- Downstream nodes do not execute unless they have an alternate active input path
- Either approach avoids ambiguous “pass-through” behavior and keeps execution predictable.

## Expected Behavior
- Disabled nodes:
  - Are not executed
  - Do not trigger API calls or LLM usage
  - Preserve configuration and placement on the canvas
- Re-enabling a node restores execution and connections instantly
- Disabled state persists across save/load
- Clear visual indicators (grayed out, dashed border, icon overlay)

## Why This Matters
This feature would significantly improve:
- Debugging workflows
- Safe experimentation
- Cost control for LLM/tool-heavy flows
- Readability and maintainability of complex flows
This is a standard capability in mature visual programming and orchestration tools and would be a major quality-of-life improvement for Flowise power users.

Whether this works depends on **both Flowise and the model/provider**.

From what I can tell:

- Flowise has added **reasoning support** in recent releases. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
- However, **streaming reasoning ("thinking") is only possible if the provider and model expose reasoning tokens/events through their API**. Flowise can't stream reasoning that the upstream API doesn't send.

```json
{
  "reasoning": {
    "enabled": true
  }
}
```

### 1. The selected OpenRouter model doesn't expose reasoning

Not every model on OpenRouter supports reasoning, and among those that do, not all expose the reasoning trace or stream it back to clients.

Some models only use internal reasoning and return the final answer.

### 2. OpenRouter may not stream reasoning content

Even if a model supports reasoning, OpenRouter must forward those reasoning events in its streaming API. I couldn't find documentation confirming that all reasoning-capable models stream their thinking through OpenRouter.

### 3. Flowise may not yet render streaming reasoning

I also couldn't find documentation stating that Flowise currently displays streamed reasoning tokens from OpenRouter in the chat UI. It's possible Flowise only consumes the final completion even when reasoning is enabled.

### Things to verify

- Which **Flowise version** are you using?
- Which **OpenRouter model** are you testing? (e.g. `qwen`, `deepseek`, `gpt-5`, `claude`, etc.)
- Does the same model return reasoning if you call the OpenRouter API directly (outside of Flowise)?

If it **does** stream reasoning via the raw OpenRouter API but **not** through Flowise, that would suggest a Flowise integration limitation or bug.

If it **doesn't** stream reasoning via the raw API either, then the limitation is likely with the selected model or OpenRouter's implementation rather than Flowise.

So, at this point I would first verify whether the behavior exists outside Flowise before concluding it's a Flowise issue.

nodes.title: Issue: Enabling Context Window Size Makes Redis Return Outdated Messages
nodes.body:
### Issue:
When using Redis as memory storage in Flowise and enabling a context window, the memory returned to the agent does not contain the latest messages.
Instead, Flowise is returning the oldest messages stored in Redis.

This breaks agent continuity because the conversation is rebuilt with outdated context.

### Expected behavior:
When context window is enabled, Flowise should discard the oldest messages, keeping only the lastest X messages (according to the k setted surface window) Example of correct behavior:

const recentMessages = allMessages.slice(-windowSize);

Return the last messages first so the agent gets the most recent conversation state

### Current behavior:
Flowise appears to apply the slice logic incorrectly, keeping the messages from the start of the array (oldest ones).
As a result, the agent receives outdated context and responds incorrectly, because:

The final messages of the conversation are missing

The model thinks the conversation is still in an old state

Multi-agent workflows break (they depend on recent context)

### Steps to reproduce:

Enable Redis as memory storage

Set a context window size (e.g. 10 messages)

Have a conversation with more than 10 interactions

The agent will only receive the first 10 stored messages — not the latest 10

### Impact:
This affects:

Multi-agent systems

Chatflows using Supervisor Agents

Agents that make decisions based on recent context

It makes Redis memory unreliable for production usage with Flowise.

nodes.title: AgentFlows Chatbot Showing Old Conversations Mid-Session (Context Reset / Glitch)
nodes.body:
Hi, I'm building a chatbot using Flowise AgentFlows, and I’m facing a recurring issue where the chatbot suddenly shows older chat messages and responses from previous sessions, even after clearing the session.

The problem occurs mid-conversation:

I ask a new question

AgentFlows starts processing

Suddenly, the UI displays old chat logs from a previous run

Or it mixes old responses with the current one

It seems like the internal memory / session store is leaking or not resetting reliably.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0c1343d4-5f40-46bd-b72e-8ef0ea5f6a67

@Kushiqtx 
What you're describing **doesn't sound like expected AgentFlows behavior**. A cleared or new session should not suddenly rehydrate messages from an unrelated conversation midway through processing.

From what I can tell, this is likely one of three things:

1. **The same `sessionId` (or `chatId`) is being reused**, so the agent is loading existing conversation history.
2. **Memory is backed by a persistent store** (Redis, database, etc.) that isn't being cleared when you think it is.
3. **A bug/regression in AgentFlows** where the UI or memory layer is restoring stale messages.

### Things to check

#### 1. Verify you're creating a new session

If you're calling the Prediction API yourself, ensure each new conversation uses a unique `sessionId` (and `chatId` if applicable). Reusing these identifiers will intentionally associate the request with the previous conversation history. Flowise uses session identifiers to maintain conversational state. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

#### 2. Check the memory configuration

If your Agent node has memory enabled (Buffer Memory, Redis Memory, etc.), verify:

- the correct session key is being used,
- memory is actually cleared when starting a new conversation,
- no external persistence layer is restoring old messages.

A mismatch between the UI session and the memory session is a common cause of "old conversations" appearing unexpectedly.

#### 3. Determine whether it's a UI or backend issue

A useful test is to inspect the execution trace or the API response:

- If the API response already contains old messages, the issue is likely in the backend/memory.
- If the API response is correct but the UI suddenly displays previous messages, the problem is more likely in the frontend state management.

This helps narrow down where the stale context is being introduced.

#### 4. Test with memory disabled

As a quick isolation step:

- disable memory on the Agent,
- start a completely new session,
- see if the issue still occurs.

If the problem disappears, it's strong evidence that the memory/session layer is involved rather than the AgentFlow execution itself.

### If this is reproducible...

If you're consistently seeing previous conversations injected into a brand-new session—even with unique session IDs—that would point to a probable AgentFlows bug rather than expected behavior.

To help reproduce it, it would be useful to share:

- Flowise version
- Self-hosted or Cloud
- Memory type (Buffer, Redis, Database, etc.)
- Whether you're using the built-in chat UI or the Prediction API
- Whether every new conversation gets a fresh `sessionId`/`chatId`
- Whether the stale messages appear in the API response or only in the UI

Those details should make it much easier to determine whether this is a configuration issue or a regression in AgentFlows.

If this solves your problem, feel free to mark it as the accepted answer so others can find it easily.

nodes.title: MCP Client – Capabilities Always Empty ({}) and Missing MCP 2024-11-05 Features
nodes.body:
# MCP Client – Capabilities Always Empty (`{}`) and Missing MCP 2024-11-05 Features

Hi Flowise team,

I recently developed several MCP servers following the **MCP 2024-11-05 specification**, and I hit a limitation when integrating them with Flowise.

Flowise sends the following `initialize` request:

```json
{
  "method": "initialize",
  "params": {
    "protocolVersion": "2024-11-05",
    "capabilities": {},
    "clientInfo": {
      "name": "flowise-client",
      "version": "1.0.0"
    }
  },
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 0
}
```

This means that **Flowise announces no MCP capabilities at all**.

As a result, only very simple tool invocation works, while the rest of the MCP spec is not supported.

---

## Missing MCP Features

Based on my tests and the Flowise codebase, the MCP client currently does **not** implement:

- `prompts/list`, `getPrompt`
- `resources/list`, resource streaming
- `completions`, `sampling`
- MCP over HTTP transport
- Capability negotiation
- Dynamic registration

Environment variable:

```
CUSTOM_MCP_PROTOCOL = sse  #(stdio | sse)
```

…only switches the transport, not the capabilities.

---

## Question

**Is there any configuration to extend the MCP capabilities declared by the Flowise MCP client?**

Or alternatively:

**Is there a planned evolution toward fuller MCP 2024-11-05 support (prompts, resources, completions, HTTP, etc.)?**

At the moment, Flowise always announces:

```json
"capabilities": {}
```

…which prevents compliant MCP servers from exposing anything beyond basic tools.

---

## Thanks

Flowise already does an impressive job as an orchestrator.  
I’d love to use it with full MCP features, and I’m happy to help test or contribute if needed.

nodes.title: Integrating file attachments in Flowise chatflow for Jira Service Management tickets
nodes.body:
Hi,

I have a chatflow that collects preliminary information before opening a support ticket and then passes it to an agentflow, which handles sending the ticket to the correct agent and finally creating a ticket in Jira Service Management by api rest.

I would like there to be an option to attach a file, but with the Flowise interface, I see that it parses them as text to attach to the LLM.

Is there any way to achieve this?

Thanks in advance.

@pferrer-pdpaola 
Yes, but not directly through the default Flowise file upload behavior.

The behavior you're seeing is expected: when a file is uploaded through the Flowise chat interface, it is typically **processed as input for the LLM/RAG pipeline** (e.g. extracted into text or embedded), rather than being preserved as a binary attachment that can later be forwarded to another system. The Uploads documentation explains that uploaded files are either parsed for RAG or made available to supported model providers, depending on your chatflow configuration. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

If your goal is:

```
User
   ↓
Upload PDF / Image / Log file
   ↓
Collect ticket information
   ↓
Create Jira Service Management ticket
   ↓
Attach the ORIGINAL file
```

then you'll need to keep the original file, not just its extracted text.

### A couple of approaches

#### Option 1 (Recommended): Use the Attachments API

Flowise provides an **Attachments API** that accepts uploaded files and can return metadata (and optionally the content/base64). This gives you a way to manage uploaded files separately from the LLM context. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

Your flow could look like:

```
Frontend
    ↓
POST /attachments/{chatflowId}/{chatId}
    ↓
Store attachment metadata
    ↓
Prediction API
    ↓
AgentFlow
    ↓
Jira REST API
```

Instead of relying on the parsed text that Flowise injects into the prompt, keep a reference to the uploaded file and use that when creating the Jira ticket.

#### Option 2: Handle uploads outside Flowise

Another common pattern is:

1. Upload the file to your own backend or object storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS, etc.).
2. Pass only the file URL or identifier into Flowise.
3. When the AgentFlow creates the Jira ticket, download the file (or read it from storage) and attach it using Jira's REST API.

This keeps the LLM focused on the conversation while preserving the original binary file.

### Creating the Jira attachment

Jira Service Management's REST API supports adding attachments, but it expects the **actual file** (multipart upload), not extracted text. Depending on the API you're using, you either:

- upload directly to the issue, or
- for JSM customer requests, upload a temporary attachment first and then associate it with the request. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

### One thing to verify

How are you creating the Jira ticket today?

- Using an **HTTP Request / REST API node**?
- A **Custom Tool**?
- An **MCP server**?

That will determine the cleanest way to carry the uploaded file (or its reference) from the chatflow into the AgentFlow and ultimately into Jira.

If this solves your problem, feel free to mark it as the accepted answer so others can find it easily.

nodes.title: Best practise for automization of data for large number of document stores
nodes.body:
Hi everyone!
We've been using flowise with great success for almost a year now in a project, that is getting pretty large now. Without the flexibility and power of Agentflows v2 we wouldn't be able to do that and scale so easy, so thanks for that awesome improvement!

Our challenge is that we have an increasing number of document stores (currently 50, one document loader per document store), 3 mio to 21 mio characters per document store and about 1500 total chunks per doc store. We use postgres as a vector db currently.

With each new document loader, the time to process and upsert documents increases. I think to process and upsert every document loader takes about 5-6 hours, one by one. Currently because of the issue with pgvector and the record manager not clearing up everything properly, we need to upsert everything all the time. And we need to do that on a regular basis, as our data changes regularly as well.

We are using Cypress to automize this and also be able to track in detail if there is an issue for a specific document loader and what might be the reason for it. Sometimes we have the issue that the Flowise UI is not responding or the processing took too long etc. In general it works fine, but we expect the project to further grow to maybe few hundred document stores. Our current approach is not ideal and we want to improve it.

I am curious if others have best practises for automizing lots of document stores/document loaders with regular data updates. 
Or maybe features are planned to make this easier and/or faster. I saw that there is already a feature on the roadmap: "Cron Job For Upsert/Refresh Doc Store, AgentflowV2". This could make things a bit easier I assume.

So I am looking forward for any input, ideas and would like to hear how you do it in your projects.

@HenryUSU 
First of all, it's great to hear you've been running Flowise successfully at that scale. **50 document stores with millions of characters each** is already beyond what many deployments handle, so you've probably reached the point where UI-driven ingestion becomes the bottleneck rather than the vector database itself.

A few suggestions that I'd consider for a deployment of this size:

### 1. Move away from UI automation where possible

Using Cypress works, but you're effectively automating a browser to trigger backend operations. Since Flowise exposes **Document Store Upsert** and **Refresh** APIs, I'd recommend driving ingestion directly via the API instead. This tends to be more reliable and easier to monitor than UI automation. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

For example, instead of:

```
Cypress
    ↓
Browser
    ↓
Flowise UI
```

consider:

```
Scheduler
    ↓
Your ingestion service
    ↓
POST /document-store/refresh/{id}
```

or

```
POST /document-store/upsert/{id}
```

This also makes retries and logging much easier.

---

### 2. Refresh only the document stores that changed

If your source systems can tell you which datasets changed, only call the Refresh API for those document stores instead of processing all 50 every run.

That can significantly reduce processing time if only a subset of your data changes regularly. Flowise's Refresh API is designed to reprocess existing document loaders within a document store. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

---

### 3. Make sure the Record Manager cleanup mode matches your workflow

You mentioned having to rebuild everything because of the current pgvector/Record Manager issue.

Normally, the Record Manager is intended to avoid unnecessary re-embedding by hashing chunks and only indexing changes. Depending on your use case, **Incremental Cleanup** is generally preferable for continuously evolving datasets, while **Full Cleanup** is intended for complete replacements. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

If you're forced to perform full re-upserts due to the pgvector issue, I'd keep an eye on fixes for that rather than optimizing around the workaround.

---

### 4. Parallelize cautiously

If your infrastructure allows it, consider refreshing multiple independent document stores concurrently (with a sensible concurrency limit).

For example:

```
Refresh Store A
Refresh Store B
Refresh Store C
```

instead of strictly serial execution.

The optimal concurrency depends on:

- embedding provider rate limits,
- PostgreSQL/pgvector capacity,
- CPU available for parsing/chunking.

Running everything in parallel usually isn't ideal, but a small worker pool often improves throughput substantially.

---

### 5. Separate ingestion from serving

At your scale, I'd treat ingestion as a dedicated background process:

```
Source systems
        ↓
Change detection
        ↓
Queue
        ↓
Workers
        ↓
Flowise Document Store API
```

This gives you retries, monitoring, and better fault isolation than a long-running browser automation job.

---

### Regarding the roadmap

I also noticed the roadmap item you mentioned for **Cron Job for Upsert/Refresh Doc Store**. From what I can tell, that would simplify scheduling inside Flowise, but it likely wouldn't change the underlying indexing performance—it would mainly reduce the operational overhead of orchestrating refreshes yourself.

---

One question: are your 50 document stores **completely independent knowledge bases**, or are they partitioned versions of the same dataset (e.g., one per customer/tenant)? If it's the latter, there may be opportunities to consolidate ingestion while filtering at retrieval time, which could reduce the number of separate upsert jobs you need to manage.

If this solves your problem, feel free to mark it as the accepted answer so others can find it easily.

# Flowise Local Adaptation Guide

> **Use Case**: Standalone Docker Desktop + Local Filesystem Access
> **Last Updated**: 2025-12-10
> **Adapted Version**: Flowise 3.012

---

## 📋 Overview

Starting from version 3.0.6, Flowise has enhanced its security measures, but these restrictions are overly strict for **standalone local environments**. This document records two critical modifications to adapt Flowise for local application scenarios.

### Use Cases
- **Local Docker Desktop**: Local development and data maintenance
- **Requirement**: Access absolute paths within containers (e.g., `/data/...`, `/app/files/...`)

---

## 🔧 Modification 1: Allow Absolute Paths in Containers

### Problem Description
Flowise 3.0.6+ introduced strict path validation that blocks all paths containing `/`, preventing the use of absolute paths within containers.

**Error Message**:
```
[ERROR]: Invalid folder path: Path traversal detected.
Please provide a safe folder path.
```

**Affected Features**:
- Folder with Files document loader
- Local filesystem access (e.g., `/data/documents/folder`)

### Official Security Background
- **Vulnerability ID**: GHSA-99pg-hqvx-r4gf (CVSS 9.1)
- **Affected Version**: 3.0.5
- **Fixed Version**: 3.0.6+
- **Issue**: The official fix is overly strict, falsely rejecting legitimate container absolute paths

### Solution

**File Location**: `packages/components/src/validator.ts`

**Lines to Modify**: Lines 31-46

#### Before (Official Version)
```typescript
export const isPathTraversal = (path: string): boolean => {
    // Check for common path traversal patterns
    const dangerousPatterns = [
        '..', // Directory traversal
        '/', // Root directory ← Too strict, blocks all absolute paths!
        '\\', // Windows root directory
        '%2e', // URL encoded .
        '%2f', // URL encoded /
        '%5c' // URL encoded \
    ]

    return dangerousPatterns.some((pattern) => path.toLowerCase().includes(pattern))
}
```

#### After (Local Adaptation)
```typescript
export const isPathTraversal = (path: string): boolean => {
    // Allow absolute paths in Linux containers (e.g., /data/...)
    // but block directory traversal attempts
    const dangerousPatterns = [
        /\.\./,                 // Directory traversal (..)
        /%2e%2e/i,              // URL encoded ..
        /%2f\.\./i,             // URL encoded /../
        /%5c/i,                 // URL encoded \ (Windows path)
        /\0/,                   // Null bytes
        /^[a-zA-Z]:\\/,         // Windows absolute paths (C:\) - not allowed in Linux containers
        /^\\\\[^\\]/,           // UNC paths (\\server\) - not allowed in Linux containers
        /%00/i                  // URL encoded null byte
    ]

    return dangerousPatterns.some((pattern) => pattern.test(path))
}
```

### Comparison

| Path Example | Official | Adapted | Description |
|--------------|----------|---------|-------------|
| `/data/documents/folder` | ❌ Blocked | ✅ Allowed | Legitimate container absolute path |
| `/root/.flowise` | ❌ Blocked | ✅ Allowed | Flowise default data directory |
| `../../../etc/passwd` | ✅ Blocked | ✅ Blocked | Path traversal attack |
| `/../../etc/passwd` | ✅ Blocked | ✅ Blocked | Path traversal attack |
| `%2e%2e/etc/passwd` | ✅ Blocked | ✅ Blocked | URL encoded traversal |
| `C:\Windows\System32` | ❌ Blocked | ✅ Blocked | Windows path (not applicable to Linux containers) |

---

## 🔧 Modification 2: Run Container as Root User

### Problem Description
Flowise 3.012 defaults to switching to a non-root user (`node`), which conflicts with the `/root/.flowise` mount configuration in `docker-compose.yml`.

**Symptoms**:
- `whoami` shows `node` instead of `root`
- Permission issues preventing access to `/root/.flowise`

### Solution

**File Location**: `Dockerfile` (root directory)

**Lines to Modify**: Lines 38 and 41

#### Before (Official Version)
```dockerfile
# Give the node user ownership of the application files
RUN chown -R node:node .

# Switch to non-root user (node user already exists in node:20-alpine)
USER node

EXPOSE 3000

CMD [ "pnpm", "start" ]
```

#### After (Local Adaptation)
```dockerfile
# Give the node user ownership of the application files
# RUN chown -R node:node .

# Switch to non-root user (node user already exists in node:20-alpine)
# USER node

EXPOSE 3000

CMD [ "pnpm", "start" ]
```

### Verification
```bash
# Enter the container
docker exec -it <container_id> sh

# Check current user
whoami
# Should output: root (not node)
```

---

## 🚀 Apply Modifications

### 1. Clone or Update Flowise Source
```bash
git clone https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise.git
cd Flowise
```

### 2. Apply Modifications

**Manual Modification:**
1. Edit `packages/components/src/validator.ts` (refer to Modification 1 above)
2. Edit `Dockerfile` (refer to Modification 2 above)

### 3. Rebuild Docker Image
```bash
docker build --no-cache -t flowise .
```

### 4. Stop Old Container
```bash
# View container ID
docker ps

# Stop old container
docker stop <container_id>

# Remove old container (optional)
docker rm <container_id>
```

### 5. Run New Container
```bash
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 \
  -v /path/to/your/data:/data \
  -e DATABASE_PATH=/data/database \
  -e APIKEY_PATH=/data/apikey \
  -e SECRETKEY_PATH=/data/secretkey \
  flowise
```

**Note**: Replace `/path/to/your/data` with your actual local path.
